title: Racial prejudice faced by Black musicians
summary: Goodwin recalls being unwelcome in rooms and Smith's mixed band in white rooms about 1961-62; Lovett says Louisiana was harsh.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Crook, so the answer is yes on that question. I would like one quick question. We don't have too much time left on this tape. Crook, you and I were walking into a room where we were playing one night and you told me
that you could remember when you weren't allowed to go near that room because you were black, some 35 years ago, maybe longer.
What, very briefly, racial prejudice as a musician, band musician in those days -- I'm afraid we don't -- how bad was it, Crook?

Well, it was very bad but you've got to remember the black musician did have some pride. He thought this way, you know, 'Well, if you don't want me in there, well I don't want to play in there, you know'. So it's just that simple. You had other places you could play.
Well you did run into it though?
Oh yes, had a place where I played with your band that 35 years ago I would have had a hard time delivering a package in there.

Yeah, you told me. I get credit for having the first mixed band in white rooms in this city; mixed and I never realized that until the agent at that time, who was Tommy Reed, told me, and you backed -- you confirmed that down at the local because I checked with you to make sure because I couldn't believe that in that day and age, 1961, '62, but you said that's true.
Now Baby, how about racial prejudice with you and make it fast, Baby, because we're running out of tape?
Well I don't have any racial prejudice.
No, I know you don't, but did you run into it?
Oh plenty of times. Around in Louisiana man, it was sharp.
I should have got onto this earlier.
Oh yeah. It was two guys going to the electric chair.
I want to tell you about it.
